Far Cry 3: Blood Dragon is a standalone expansion developed by Ubisoft Montreal. Built on the mechanics of Far Cry 3, it transforms the tropical shooter into a neon-soaked 1980s action parody. It’s a self-contained experience that celebrates and mocks the era’s sci-fi clichés with style and humor.

Gameplay retains the core Far Cry formula: open-ended combat, stealth takedowns, and light progression. Players control Sergeant Rex “Power” Colt, a cyber commando sent to eliminate a rogue army on a retro-futuristic island. The structure mirrors Far Cry 3’s sandbox but compresses it into a smaller, more focused world.

Combat is fast, chaotic, and exaggerated. Enemies burst into neon sparks, explosions light up the horizon, and every weapon feels overpowered in the best way. The bow, shotgun, and laser rifle offer satisfying variety, while takedowns remain fluid and rewarding. Stealth is still viable, but the tone encourages loud, destructive play.

Visually, Blood Dragon is striking. The world glows with neon lighting, purple skies, and scan-line effects that emulate VHS-era aesthetics. The interface and HUD pulse with retro energy, and every visual choice supports the parody theme without breaking functionality.

The soundtrack by Power Glove is essential to the experience. Heavy synth beats and rhythmic basslines perfectly capture the feel of 1980s action cinema. Combined with intentionally over-the-top dialogue and one-liners, the game nails its comedic tone without overstaying its welcome.

The campaign lasts around six hours, balancing exploration and set-piece missions. Side activities like base captures and collectibles add replay value, but the pacing keeps the experience tight. The simplified progression system ensures constant power growth without grinding.

Overall, Far Cry 3: Blood Dragon is a focused, stylish reinvention of the Far Cry formula. It turns familiar mechanics into a celebration of retro absurdity—fun, fast, and self-aware. It’s short but perfectly tuned for what it aims to be: a neon homage to 80s action that never takes itself seriously and never stops being entertaining.

Do yourself a favor and check the guides section to keep Blood Dragon from wasting your time attempting to connect to Ubisoft servers for 30 seconds at a time whenever you load up or pause the game. The opening of Blood Dragon actually mocks controlling tutorials and HUDs, so it's pitifully shameful and embarrassing of Ubisoft to have to manually remove their controlling BS from this game.

Once that's taken care of, there is a fun experience here! Far Cry 3 Blood Dragon delivers exceptionally well as a parody of the 80's masculinity and conservative power fantasies that dominated the action films and DTV titles of the 80's and early 90's. Tough guys, stupid one-liners and posturing, neon-everything, future-everything, cybernetics, etc. It's also packing a lot of other 80's and early 90's references to genuinely good films that stand the test of time. All of this is packaged with a respectable amount of cutscenes done in the style of an 80's arcade or NES game with really solid voice acting. Very entertaining stuff!

Gameplay holds up better than some. Eventually, I did get bored with the bullet sponge enemies and the piss-poor accuracy of our cyber commando protagonist. Bad accuracy makes it tedious to kill enemies with weapons fire, tedious to reload, and really annoying that Blood Dragon pushes an ammo conservation mechanic that involves acquiring and spending money to buy ammo at vending machine stores throughout the game. Fortunately, it's nothing some cheats can't fix. I only use cheats when a game is entering the realm of 'no fun.' I did that here as this is a game that is dated in a way that wasn't designed to hold up.

For a standalone Far Cry 3 spin off, and despite the short main story questline, there's a lot of side missions and extra content packed in here! The game is too dated for me to want to play through it all, but respectable!

My recommendation would be play it for the entertainment value of an 80's parody that revels in the fun and ridiculous nature of it all, and that's it.

Far Cry 3 Blood Dragon was a meme spinoff that came out at the start of the 80s nostalgia revival 10 years ago. For as old as the title is, the aesthetic and lighting alone allow it to hold up to modern standards. It is by far the most streamlined Far Cry experience, barely any collectibles, small map, you can take out every outpost right away and in only a couple of hours, short campaign. This is a strength to the game at its low cost because it does not overstay its welcome and never gets boring or monotonous like future Far Cry titles could get when Ubisoft games became full on bloatware. Rex can move as fast as a car and has most of the skills unlocked, you can unlock things like more hit points and heavy takedowns after leveling up but if you are skilled enough you can beat the game in an hour or two. 
Blood Dragon is a goofy title that tries to make the most out of its 80s action movie cheesy throwback nature while being both over the top stupid and charming at the same time. Michael Biehn does a great job channeling his 80s action career highlights into his role as Rex Power Colt with his performance being memorable enough that I still remembered it 10 years after release. If you like Far Cry at all and have not played this title, it is worth it if it is on sale.

        [td]FC3 Blood Dragon has a pretty cool artstyle. It gives this old school 80’s Sci Fi vibe that not many games really represent.         [td]🎮Gameplay[/td]
        [td]The gameplay is fun! It’s fast paced and has good gunplay. Far Cry always had solid gunplay anyway. The map is open world, so there is some exploration. All over the map you have these enemy outposts you can destroy, and once you do, you can use them as fast travel points. The enemies (even on hardmode) are pretty easy. This game didn’t really have much of a challenge. The only time this game gets tough is when you face the dragons. They are super tanky and cause a ton of damage. They are also surprisingly common on the map, which in my opinion, can be freaking annoying. Side quests are a thing in this game, and they do reward you with weapon upgrades. I mean it’s cool to see weapon upgrades, but most of them are mainly buffs and don’t really change the weapons that much. There is stealth in this game, but I never really used it, just sparingly. If you love stealth, then you might like it on here, although it’s super basic. Now I do feel a bit conflicted with the exploration. To be honest, it was kinda hard for me to get into this map. Most of the map just looked the same and didn’t really have any interesting locations. I guess I got spoiled by more modern open world maps, I'm not sure. It was just dull. Overall, the gameplay is solid. Nothing wild or unique, but still fun.[/td]

Okay, in all seriousness, I might prefer the grit and immersion of 2, but Far Cry 3: Blood Dragon and the original Far Cry 3 are easily the best of the Far Cry series from an objective point of view, and after rightfully sitting out the new low point of the series that is Far Cry 6, playing Blood Dragon feels like a reminder of what made 2 & 3 so great to begin with: An open world shooter, with activities to partake in, fearsome [though samey] enemies, and an excellent arsenal of firepower. 
Blood Dragon however takes it up a notch with not just THE best selection of weapons in the series, but by being incredibly funny in its affectionate lampooning of 1980s Sci-Fi and Action. The tone is fittingly comedic and silly, with even the descriptions for the weapons and wildlife being written in a tongue-in-cheek manner. 
Highlights include the actual tutorial, the hilarious death of a certain character early on, the mad ramblings of sexually-deprived Doctor Carlyle, the combative nature of the AIs, even your protagonist can get you laughing! 

It's honestly, one of the funniest games I've ever played, and also a damn fine shooter on top of that. The games don't connect to one another plot-wise, but you should DEFINITELY buy both Far Cry 3 and this expansion, because both deliver some of the finest shooter gameplay and writing of the 2010s. And yes, Blood Dragon IS much better than Captain Laserhawk.

The game is pretty badass for a quick playthrough. You play as "Rex" who is a cyber-commando so you're basically the terminator and you're OP. Compared to Far Cry 3, in this game you don't take fall damage, enemies are easier to kill, you have more health, and have really powerful weapons/attachments available to you. The voice lines that Rex has is sometimes quite funny, so you can tell the developers had some fun making this game. It is basically like one of those retro arcade games from the 1980s where your character is near invincible and you just obliterate everything in your path. I enjoyed it even if it was only for a short amount of time and it was interesting to experience for the first time. 

In my opinion, I think $15 is a little much for what the game offers. Therefore, I'd only recommend this game when it is on sale. The only dislike I have on this game is the stupid message that would pop up anytime I paused the game or went to the menu that said "Please wait while we connect to Far Cry 3 Blood Dragon servers". I blame this on Ubisoft connect because it is typically what to blame in moments like this. I'm sure there's an easy work-around to it, but I always just waited 10 seconds for it to go away every time it popped up because it didn't mess up anything other than the flow of the game.

First off, let's talk about the protagonist, Rex Colt. He's the embodiment of every action hero stereotype imaginable. He's got a gravelly voice that sounds like he gargles with motor oil, muscles so big they have their own zip codes, and a personality as subtle as a sledgehammer. Oh, and did I mention he's a cyborg? Because of course, he is! Because in the '80s, why settle for just being a regular tough guy when you could be a regular tough guy with lasers shooting out of your eyeballs?

The story? Well, it's basically every '80s action movie plot rolled into one glorious mess. You've got evil scientists, mutant creatures, and a villain so over-the-top evil that even Cobra Commander would tell him to dial it down a notch. It's like the game designers took a blender, threw in every action movie cliché they could find, hit puree, and then added a healthy dose of neon pink just for good measure. My only complaint is that there's absolutely no achievements for this on Steam.

Gameplay Mechanics – How the game plays moment-to-moment (movement, controls, unique systems).

This game is made directly from Far Cry 3, so most of the game mechanics are the same, but kinda enhanced since in this one you are a cyber soldier that is 85% synthetic. In this game you can run A LOT faster, which is highly appreciated as it makes walking through the not-so-big map looking for the collectibles quite quick. You can jump, climb take ziplines, ride cars, boats and jet-ski's as well as gliders (sadly no wingsuit). You can also swim real fast, which is very satisfying.

There is not fall damage!

Difficulty & Challenge – How hard the game is, balance of challenge, fairness.

I played on easy since I knew this game did not take itself too seriously and I don't like the Far Cry games difficulty scaling in general. It was quite easy, like I was Doomslayer in Far Cry. You get a lot of health in this game so I think that even in higher difficulties it should be easier than base Far Cry 3.

Combat System – How fights feel, variety of moves, enemy behavior.

The combat plays exactly like Far Cry three. You get a Pistol, Shot gun, AR, Sniper, Bow, Flamethrower and a Laser arm thingy. Most guns have some attachments that are quite fun, like making the sniper shots explosive or make the shotgun throw napalm bullets.

For throwables you have Dice that can distract enemies, Molotov Cocktails, Grenades and Cyber hearts. The hearts are a throwable that you actually loot from the soldiers you kill, and they are used to lure the weird looking wingless Dragons.

You can also perform stealth takedowns and by doing them you insta loot money and hearts.

For healing you get a syringe and also the less effective self repairs you can do on yourself. The animations for those are quite funny and cool.

Weapons, Gear & Abilities – Variety, upgrade systems, usefulness, uniqueness.

I already talked mostly everything on the weapons on the combat section.

The game has some passive skills you get by leveling up, but weirdly enough you don't select them yourself, you just acquire them with levels. Therefore i have no idea what they do, as I never opened the menu to look at them, I just accepted.

Level/Area/Mob Design – How environments are structured, exploration, layout creativity.

The map is quite small, which is a good thing for this game as there is not much content. Around the map you can find the strongholds you need to conquer quite evenly spaced out. There are a few caves you gotta go to find some collectibles. The look of the world is quite bland, but sometimes you fin one interesting structure just in the middle of nowhere. But mostly it is jungle and the regular Far Cry facilities with the same materials.

There are not a lot of mobs, there is even an achievement to headshot each type of enemy. There are the enemy soldiers that have sub categories, Elite enemy soldiers, Friendly scientist guys, Dragons, One friendly NPC soldier guy and a few zombie like mobs. On top of that you get mutated versions of Far Cry 3 animals.

There are also enemies on boats, heli's and cars. I love that you can kill the heli pilot and the chopper just falls from the sky.

Story & Narrative – Plot, characters, pacing, emotional impact.

The story is quite cheesy and fun at times. It is basically: you are Rex, a cyber soldier that is trying to stop a guy from using dragon blood to make weapons and unleash chaos in all continents. Rex is just happy to be there, kill stuff and blow up things, spouting one liners WHENEVER he feels like it, sometimes it lands but sometimes it becomes repetitive (mainly when chasing collectibles and killing with the specific guns). The tutorial is presented in a very self aware fourth wall way, and this happens sometimes through the story. There also is a borderlands style of humor to the dialogue.

There are secondary missions that are always Hunt an animal or Rescue a scientist hostage. Doing this side quests unlock attachments for the weapons.

Visuals & Art Style – Graphics quality, artistic direction, animations.

I am not gonna lie, the game is quite damn ugly. It has that CRT tv effect and it is night the whole time. The strongholds have a constant beam of light polluting the sky. The cutscenes are very arcade retro looking. I get that it is the intention to make it look like you're playing an arcade machine, but still, it was not done tastefully. The dragons look like weird lizards with no wings and that is a weird choice in my opinion. But yeah, the constant darkness is quite dull.

Performance & Polish – Bugs, frame rate, loading times, overall smoothness.

The game ran fine for me, and I did not encounter any bugs.

Replayability – Side content, multiple endings, NG+ options.

There is none. this is a one and done game. There is no reason to play this twice.

Boss Fights – Design, difficulty, creativity, memorability.

I guess you kinda could call the dragons the bosses of the games, because, sadly, we don't fight the big bad guy of the game. He just appears in the Cutscenes. The dragons have a weak spot in the chest and are able to throw huge lasers from the mouth, quite nice to fight, but nothing special. The late game weapons obliterate them.

Achievements – Creativity, difficulty, how they encourage exploration or mastery.

This is a regular Far Cry achievement list. Finish the game, do side quests, collect the collectibles. Not bad at all, if you always loot the money from enemies during you playthrough you won't need to grind money at all. You can buy the maps for the collectible locations by liberating strongholds and that's wonderful as it makes you not need to keep checking a guide to find everything. The collectible hunt is quick.

Overall a 6/10 Game. Fun and enjoyable for a single run with a few solid moments of humor. This is borderlands light.

**1. Long Play Review: Far Cry 3 - Blood Dragon**

**Intro:** Far Cry 3 - Blood Dragon, developed by Ubisoft Montreal, is a standalone expansion to Far Cry 3 that takes the series in a wildly different, neon-drenched, 80s-inspired direction.  Playing as Sergeant Rex "Power" Colt, a cyber-commando, you're on a mission to stop Colonel Sloan and his cyber-soldiers from unleashing a nuclear apocalypse.  Prepare for over-the-top action, cheesy one-liners, and a healthy dose of nostalgia. 🤖

**Gameplay:** Blood Dragon takes the core gameplay of Far Cry 3 and amplifies it to absurd levels.  You'll still be exploring an open world, taking down outposts, hunting wildlife (now cybernetically enhanced), and completing missions.  However, the focus here is less on realism and more on pure, unadulterated fun.  You'll have access to ridiculous weapons, like the KillStar, and can even ride laser-breathing dragons.  The game's short length keeps the action from becoming stale, and the constant stream of 80s references and cheesy humor keeps things entertaining. 💥

**Story & World:** Blood Dragon's story is intentionally cheesy and over-the-top, a loving parody of 80s action movies.  The world is a neon-drenched, post-apocalyptic landscape filled with cybernetic creatures, glowing flora, and plenty of opportunities for mayhem.  The game doesn't take itself seriously for a second, and that's a big part of its charm.  It's a world where logic takes a backseat to style and fun. 📜

**Graphics & Sound:** Blood Dragon's visuals are heavily stylized, with a vibrant color palette and a retro aesthetic.  The neon glow and VHS effects add to the 80s vibe.  The soundtrack is a perfect blend of synthwave and heavy metal, perfectly complementing the game's over-the-top action.  The voice acting is intentionally cheesy and hammy, adding to the game's comedic tone. 🎶

**Pros:**
* Hilarious and self-aware story that parodies 80s action movies 😂
* Over-the-top action and ridiculous weapons 💥
* Stylized visuals and a killer synthwave soundtrack 🎶
* Short and sweet gameplay that doesn't overstay its welcome ⏳
* Unique and memorable experience that stands apart from other Far Cry games 🤖

**Cons:**
* Can be too short for some players ⌛
* Gameplay mechanics are largely the same as Far Cry 3, with some minor tweaks 🔄
* Humor may not appeal to everyone 🤷
* Lacks the depth and complexity of other Far Cry titles 🧠

**Overall:** Far Cry 3 - Blood Dragon is a fantastic standalone expansion that delivers a healthy dose of nostalgia and over-the-top fun.  It's a refreshing change of pace from the more serious tone of other Far Cry games, and its short length keeps the action from becoming repetitive.  If you're looking for a fun and hilarious action game that doesn't take itself too seriously, Blood Dragon is definitely worth checking out. 8.5/10 👍

Far Cry 3: Blood Dragon is an 80s fever dream wrapped in VHS tape and soaked in synthwave. It's not a sequel, it's not a DLC — it's a standalone explosion of pure, dumb fun. Think Far Cry 3’s gameplay, but shoved through a radioactive arcade machine.

You play as Sergeant Rex "Power" Colt, a Mark IV cyber-commando voiced by none other than Michael Biehn. The story is intentionally ridiculous — a spoof of every 80s action movie and Saturday morning cartoon mashed into one gloriously cheesy package. The dialogue? So bad, it's perfect. The one-liners alone are worth the price of admission.

Gameplay is classic Far Cry with a twist: stealth kills, bow and arrows, explosions everywhere, laser guns, neon dragons that shoot lasers from their eyes, and enemy bases ripe for the taking. tl;dr it's a fun game with a campy 80s cyberpunk aesthetic that makes you feel like a bad-ass action hero. However, outside of the story quests, the game does not have that much to offer and the game does effectively nothing to prevent power creep, thereby trivializing many encounters.

[b]"The Good"[/b]
- Thematically, this game knocks it out of the park. It executes on every bad campy 80s sci-fi action movie trope perfectly and makes it feel like you are playing out a B-movie. The dialogue is cheesy in the best possible way and I could not help but have a smile on my face during every cutscene. It's like if Kung Fury was an action fps.

- The soundtrack is quite good and is one of the biggest factors which sell the aesthetic of the game. I went in expecting just a mediocre synthwave soundtrack and was instantly surprised by the quality of the menu theme. The soundtrack especially delivers [spoiler]during the final encounter[/spoiler]

- The gunplay is excellent and offers a wide arsenal of fun weapons and playstyles (except for the bow and shotgun, which feel under-powered). I have a soft spot for the Kobracon sniper rifle (especially when [spoiler]you upgrade it to have explosive rounds[/spoiler]).

[b]"The Meh"[/b]
- It is not hard to be insanely overpowered while playing this game, especially while using a certain Kobracon weapon enhancement. The game does not appear to scale enemies to match your level or your weaponry. The end result is that you can charge into a garrison like Rambo, tank all the laser bolts, and steamroll all opposition. Or you can sit in a bush outside and snipe every grunt inside the base.

There were several times I liberated a garrison in under a minute.
And I was playing on the hardest difficulty.
And I suck at fps games.

While it feels great to be an unstoppable force, I would have liked to be punished for all the times I was being cocky.

- This game does not have cinematic cutscenes, which are a missed opportunity. I like the design of the pixel-art cutscenes, but every time one happens, the gameplay is abruptly interrupted and replaced by a completely different presentation style.

- The final mission is near-perfect in my opinion. Everything comes together for a brilliant finale... and then [spoiler]the final showdown against Sloan is replaced by a cutscene. A proper bossfight would have been a perfect conclusion to the game.[/spoiler]

- The open world isn't that interesting to explore. It's pretty same-y overall.

- The AI is a little braindead at times.

- Though I liked a lot of the one-liners, I wish my character wouldn't repeat the same stock lines over and over again.

[b]"The Bad"[/b]
- Requires Ubisoft Connect and a Ubisoft account. There should be no reason for this since this game is ten years old and is basically irrelevant now.

- "Please wait while we connect you to Far Cry 3: Blood Dragon servers."
(Online features are disabled, so why is an account needed? Also this message pops up every fucking time you hit escape, it's obnoxious).

- Outside of story missions, the side quests and collectathons are so simple that they become a little dull and tedious. Moreover, they all basically play the same, so outside of the main story the game is pretty stale. If they weren't tied to weapon upgrades (and if I wasn't a completionist) I would ignore all of them. At least the mission briefs are written well.

- You see almost every enemy variation within the first hour or so of the game. Variety would have been nice...

[b]Conclusion[/b]
Overall, I would recommend the game. It fulfilled my expectations of what I wanted the game to be, however, there were a few blunders in its execution. Especially during the side-missions. It's far from being one the best fps games I've played (HL2 and ULTRAKILL are more deserving of that honor) but I had a lot of fun playing it.

[h2]Far Cry 3: Blood Dragon – A Neon-Soaked Blast from the Past[/h2] 

This is one of those games that doesn’t take itself too seriously and that’s exactly what makes it so entertaining. Set in a bizarre, retro-futuristic world inspired by 80s action movies and cartoons, this standalone spin-off of Far Cry 3 offers a wild and absurd ride that’s both hilarious and action-packed.

The story isn’t particularly deep, but it doesn’t need to be. You play as Sergeant Rex "Power" Colt, a cybernetic super-soldier on a mission to stop a rogue agent and save the world. It’s over-the-top, ridiculous, and absolutely embraces its own cheesiness. From the intentionally cringe-worthy one-liners to the synth-heavy soundtrack and endless pop culture references, the game leans hard into nostalgia and somehow, it works.

What really kept me going was the constant sense of fun. Despite its simplicity, the narrative had just enough intrigue to pull me through to the end. The humor lands more often than not, and the commitment to the aesthetic is genuinely impressive.

That said, the game isn't without its flaws. There's a noticeable amount of repetition in the missions and open-world tasks. Collectibles those ever-present Ubisoft staples felt mostly unnecessary, although I still found myself chasing them down in the name of becoming the ultimate badass. It’s a bit of a grind, but if you're in the right mood, it’s all part of the charm.

One major drawback is the bugs. There were several frustrating moments where I had to restart due to crashes or broken missions, and the lack of reliable autosaving only made things worse. In 2025, these kinds of technical issues feel especially outdated and hurt the overall experience.

Still, Far Cry 3: Blood Dragon remains a fun, quirky detour from more serious titles. It’s perfect for a quick escape between major AAA releases even today. If you can tolerate a few technical hiccups, you’re in for a memorable, neon-lit ride.

[h1]Review of Far Cry 3 Blood Dragon[/h1]
Pure 1980's action flick cheese mixed with a high octane twist on the base of Far Cry 3's open world fundamentals? Yeah it's no wonder Blood Dragon spawned a community of its own. 

Blood Dragon started a trend with the Ubisoft Far Cry titles, where we'd see a spin off game released in between the mainline titles every other year. Or at least, that's how it was for a while. From Blood Dragon prior to FC4, Primal prior to FC5, to New Dawn prior to FC6. As someone who started playing the series in 2012 with the third game, I've followed every release since. 

[u]"You know, I'm starting to actually like this.."[/u]
I'm going to be completely honest, when I first played this game many years ago, I wasn't really a fan. I replayed it a couple times back when, but it got to the point I'd consider skipping it when doing a franchise playthrough. However, my experience after replaying it just recently was completely different. I had a total blast, and I think I know why. Normally I prefer to play Ubi Far Cry titles on the hardest difficulty, Blood Dragon included. This time I decided to try Blood Dragon on a lower difficulty, and suddenly I was living my own VHS tape action movie. It's clear I found my personal sweet spot for enjoying the game after all these years. 

Blood Dragon is a 1980's synth inspired spinoff title, that heavily parodies movies of that decade. Tropes & all (Even a training & sex montage!). The story is as simple as go kill big bad & save the girl while serving lady liberty. All the while the protagonist is spouting the cheesiest one liners known to man, these of which I find hilarious. Rex "Power" Colt is a Mk.IV Cyber Commando, and he's sent to investigate Colonel Sloan, a rogue operative. Along the way he brings down Sloan's entire operation by eliminating key targets and capturing strongholds for the scientist nerds. The distant nuclear wasteland of 2007 is at threat of being reduced even further by Sloan's desire to return Humanity to a Stone Age-like existence. The key to this vision? Blood dragons. 

[u]"He said 'blow me'. So I did."[/u]
Easily the most enjoyable part of Blood Dragon for me is its gameplay. A majority of Far Cry 3's open world mechanics remain here, but most things have been tweaked in favor of a sort of power fantasy. Rex is capable of running & swimming faster than a normal Human, nor does he take fall damage. This allows you to run about the new, albeit small & somewhat bland, island with minimal restriction. 

I think my favorite part is the way leveling and weaponry works. The standard arsenal is much smaller than Far Cry 3 itself, at only 5 core weapons, and 3 additional ones you can find later on. Though this time you unlock new attachments by completing optional missions from your scientist buddies. This was an addicting process because every upgrade you obtain adds or changes something with your weapon. Visually & mechanically. The SMG going from a burst fire ballistic weapon, to a fully automatic pulse rifle with a badass reload animation was ecstasy. Or your Terminator 2 inspired lever action shotgun gaining extra barrels and new ammunition that completely deletes anything at close range. You also have the A.J.M.9, inspired by Robocop, which serves as one of your go-to stealth weapons, a sniper rifle capable of firing explosive rounds, and the classic unchanged recurve bow. The bow can't be upgraded unfortunately, however. Later you'll be able to make use of a laser minigun, flamethrower, and the greatest thing to bless our little souls.. the Killstar. Meanwhile leveling works in a more traditional sense. You don't have a skill tree, and instead obtain character upgrades as you level up to 30.

Combat works nearly identically to Far Cry 3. Enemy types are cyber variants of the archetypes you find in the base game. For better or worse. I say for worse because in my opinion this actually makes stealth harder, as the standard cyber soldiers have this giant ball shaped helmet. Even a fully upgraded burst from the handgun at point blank range can fail to pop the dome sometimes, and because this is an older FC, you'll alert the entire base failing to do so. I think that's another reason I struggled to enjoy the game originally. Opting for loud approaches here was so much fun in comparison. 

After capturing strongholds, you get a collection of side missions to do. Hunting down important targets, protecting/rescuing scientists, or the odd completely unique one like taking on a bunch of mutated sewer turtles with a taste for pizza. Hmm.. seems familiar. Scattered across the open world are also your usual fare of collectibles. This time being data notes, TV's & VHS tapes. Because of course. Hunting the cybernetic animals is also required for all unlocks and 100% completion. 

Then to the selling point of this game, the blood dragons. These big giant beasts that fire beams of destruction from their eyeballs, roam around random parts of the map. They're conceptually exciting. You can even lure them around using thrown cyber hearts, and they'll wipe out camps all on their own. Unfortunately though, these guys are a little buggy in my experience.. I'll leave that for the below section.

[u]"Come down and face me you rusty cum buckets."[/u]
Alright, so I'll briefly go over some of my issues with Blood Dragon. Even after finding a lot to enjoy, there's still some things I'm either mixed or unhappy with. 

The first and probably biggest issue I have, is the CRT filter. The entire game has this filter present. It's obviously an aesthetic choice, but it genuinely causes my eyes to strain after a while. There's no way to turn it off ingame. I've heard you can disable it in the files, so at least there's that I guess. 

Blood dragons are buggy. The most common attack they have is to blast you with their eye lasers, but every time I killed one, I would get blasted by phantom lasers every single time after their body was turned to a pile of dragon goo. 

"Service Not Available" .. ugh. After Ubisoft ended online services for various games, Blood Dragon included, you get this obnoxious pop up nearly every time you open the menu. You're forced to sit for like 30 seconds to a minute before you're given control again, and can't look at what you were trying to. I'm happy we can still play the game, but what's so hard about just putting a little pop up in the top corner when you launch that reminds you services are shut down, and not impede the pacing of gameplay with this? 

Lastly, the game is insanely short. We're talking 3-4 hours to 100% the game on high difficulties. That's not necessarily a bad thing, I just prefer games to be much longer. Thankfully, I will enjoy replaying this from now on, so I'll get to keep having fun with it. I could also add here, that there's this "Annoying Tutorial" joke at the beginning of the game, that's suppose to spoof how hand holding and interrupting game tutorials can be, which can be funny on a first time playthrough, On subsequent playthroughs it actually just is annoying because you can't skip it. A minor gripe though.

[h1]Conclusion (Pros & Cons)[/h1]
All in all, it's a great little package after enjoying Far Cry 3, or just wanting more Far Cry in general even if it's whacky and full of entertaining cheese. I'm happy I was able to find enjoyment with the game after so many years.

Far Cry 3: Blood Dragon is a fun, retro-inspired spin-off, but it doesn't quite live up to the depth or impact of Far Cry 3. The story is a lighthearted parody of 80s action films, featuring Rex Powercolt, a cybernetic super-soldier battling mutants and evil forces. While it’s amusing and filled with over-the-top humor, it lacks the emotional weight and character development of Far Cry 3, making it feel more like a diversion than a compelling narrative.

The gameplay mechanics are familiar, with open-world exploration and first-person combat, but they’re simplified. There's less emphasis on crafting and exploration, and the upgrades and combat don’t offer the same depth as in Far Cry 3. The weapons, though, are a fun mix of futuristic laser guns and flamethrowers, offering a fresh twist on the familiar formula, but the missions can get repetitive.

Visually, the game is a neon-drenched 80s dream, with bold colors and quirky details, providing a stark contrast to the more realistic world of Far Cry 3. It’s fun to look at but doesn’t offer the same immersion. The comic book-style cutscenes are a unique touch, though they might feel distracting or too simplistic for some players.

Ultimately, Blood Dragon is a fun, brief ride that offers nostalgia and humor, but it doesn’t have the same lasting appeal or complexity as its predecessor. It’s an enjoyable, light experience for fans of the series, but not something that will leave a lasting impression like Far Cry 3 did.

And compared to other similar open world games, this is pretty small in scope; a fairly small map, small range of enemies and weapons, a small set of side missions with little variety between them. Everything here is open world lite.

But that's also kind of the beauty of it. If you can pick this up cheap, then this gives you that rarest of things; a bite sized open world game. You can 100% this in a day without much difficulty. There are no filler weapons, no weak pistol you throw away when you get a stronger one; there's one Pistol, one Shotgun, one Sniper Rifle etc., and they're all fairly decent. The aesthetic obviously needs to be discussed. This is a game with neon palm trees, cybernetic panthers, guns that can be upgraded to fire lasers instead of bullets. It's a game where a level-up is met with a wailing guitar riff, as you throw the devil horns with your robot hand, electricty arching between your fingers. It's a game so filled with pulp 80s sci-fi energy, it finishes with a Miami Connection reference, for goodness sake; cuts don't get much deeper.

If you want to spend 10 hours blasting cyborgs with quad-barrel shotguns and watching 8-bit styled training montages, or if you want that open-world style of gameplay without the time investment or complexity that usually means, Blood Dragon is for you.

“The year is 2007... the apocalypse has had an apocalypse.”
Far Cry 3: Blood Dragon is what happens when a development team says, “What if we took everything from 1980s sci-fi action movies and crammed it into a game — and also made it funny as hell?” The result is a short but explosively fun standalone expansion that completely ditches Far Cry 3’s realism in favor of laser dinosaurs, cheesy one-liners, and VHS-fueled chaos.

You are Sergeant Rex “Power” Colt, a Mark IV cyber-commando voiced with maximum gravel by Michael Biehn (The Terminator, Aliens). After being dropped into a neon-soaked island crawling with mutants, killer robots, and dragons that shoot lasers from their eyes, you must stop your former commander from nuking the world… again.

The story is ridiculous on purpose, delivered in 8-bit cutscenes and overflowing with parody. It’s a love letter to ’80s B-movies and Saturday morning cartoons for adults — completely aware of how dumb it is, and loving every minute of it.

At its core, Blood Dragon is Far Cry 3 in a new skin — but what a skin it is.

Classic Gameplay, New Attitude: Expect open-world outposts, stealth takedowns, looting, and plenty of explosions — all wrapped in neon and synthwave.

No Crafting, No Grinding: You level up automatically, and weapon upgrades are earned through missions and side content. It’s streamlined, fast, and focused on fun.

Laser Guns & Explosive Bows: The arsenal is pure ‘80s excess — shotguns with explosive rounds, miniguns with infinite ammo, and sci-fi rifles that hum with power.

Blood Dragons: Giant neon reptiles that can be used as terrifying weapons… or terrifying enemies. You can even lure them into enemy bases using cyber-hearts.

Side missions include rescuing nerds, blowing up infrastructure, and liberating garrisons. It’s dumb, loud, and absurdly satisfying.

The art direction is intentionally retro-futuristic: purple skies, neon-lit rocks, glowing rivers, and scanning HUDs that wouldn’t look out of place in RoboCop. While built on the same engine as Far Cry 3, the visual overhaul gives Blood Dragon a distinct identity.

The synth-heavy soundtrack by Power Glove is phenomenal — pounding, catchy, and perfectly matched to the world’s vibe. Think John Carpenter meets Mega Man.

Voice acting leans hard into the satire, and Michael Biehn delivers every line with exactly the kind of gravelly, no-nonsense sarcasm the role demands.

Far Cry 3: Blood Dragon is a rare kind of spin-off — one that fully embraces its insanity, breaks the mold of its parent game, and becomes something completely unique. It may not be long (a focused 5–6 hour experience), but every second is packed with absurd fun, nostalgia-soaked style, and memorable moments.

This isn’t a “serious” Far Cry game — and that’s exactly why it works so well.

Recommended For:
Fans of 1980s action films, players who enjoy tongue-in-cheek humor, and those looking for a short, explosive, highly stylized shooter.

Avoid If:
You’re looking for realism, depth, or a serious story.

Far Cry 3: Blood Dragon is a neon-drenched blast of retro insanity — short, sharp, and unforgettable.

Far Cry 3: Blood Dragon puts me in a difficult position. I loved Far Cry 3, and thought the creative direction to incorporate cheesy 80's-style humor with retro gaming was a neat take. But like... when you're playing a game, and you find yourself having to purposefully push yourself to keep playing it? That's a bad sign.

I'd give a plot synopsis, but really, there's not much more to it then "you're a badass cyborg on an island killing pretty much everything while you save the world for the USA." If the humor the game uses were enough to make up for the flat plot, this might be exclusable, but there were countless groaners that really fit the genre... too well. Guys, there's a reason we don't right corny as hell plots like this anymore.

Alright, so the story is flat and schlocky, how about the gameplay? Well, it's basically just Far Cry 3, except... detached. You've got maybe 6 hours in the core game, 16ish overall if you get all the collectables. They didn't add much new until really the end of the game, and really, half of what was so fun about Far Cry 3 was you ascended your character from weak chump to badass over the course of the game, discovering new skills and abilities. Here, you just start out a badass becoming a bigger badass, fighting hordes and hordes of bland, faceless enemies... It just kind of became boring. Vast murder and tons of explosions became boring. That's half the selling point of your game!

The only stuff I really took enjoyment in was the stealth and the mobility, which is surpisingly good. The environments may not be all that pretty, but at least moving about them is a fluid and kinda pleasant experience.

All in all, unless you really want some kind of new Far Cry 3 experience? Just avoid this one. I'm surprised I stuck with it as long as I did.

"First, for those of you using Windows 10, Blood Dragon was designed pre-Windows 10 so Windows 10 is unsupported. I recommend doing things like doing a fresh install of your video card driver and windows resources and see if that fixes it."

The Short Version: widespread technical issues and incessant crashes render the game unplayable for many PC users.

The Long Version: I jumped into the stormy, explosive waters of Far Cry right with its third installment, tasting the salt and bullet baffet for the first time with Far Cry 3.
Blood Dragon's parent game was an interesting adventure and for the most part a fun ride, but both Far Cry 3 and this wacky incarnation of it seem to fail the most basic requirement of a PC game: 

...You have to be able to play it.

For that lofty goal to be achieved, it simply needs to be a thing that can run on the PC. 
Unfortunately, this is not the case for a great many PC users, myself included. 
When I first purchased Far Cry 3 (and later Blood Dragon), my computer met every single one of the minimum requirements to run it, but I haven't been able to get the game running. Technical support was of no help at all, and even after upgrading my computer (which I shouldn't have had to do, since I already met all the requirements), finally getting the game to work was an ordeal when I discovered that the game would crash on me almost every five minutes of play. Worse, it would often give me the Blue Screen of Death, forcing me to reboot. Even after trying everything I could from every advice, tip and tutorial I found online written for (and by) the many users who have gove through the exact same issues, the game would still crash. 

Since the game doesn't let you decide when you save your progress, most of my original run of Far Cry 3 was devoted to trying to get through the mandatory tutorial (that felt like it was 20-minutes long) in the beginning of the game, hoping it would not-crash long enough for me to get to a checkpoint and not have to start all over again when the game inevitably freezes my computer, forcing both a reboot on my part as well as a long wail of frustration, curled fingers reaching for the uncaring dark skies above.

Blood Dragon, I was hoping, would be an improvement and the issues with its parent game (which were reported not only by yours truly, but a great many users who practically flooded not only the official game forums but a big chunk of other threads and discussion boards) - unfortunately, the game crashed right in the middle of the (again, mandatory) tutorial in the beginning, shortly after the opening scene and before I could get two minutes into the thing.

I wish I had more to say about both games, but this abyssal experience has not allowed me much of an opportunity to actually play the game itself, and since it shouldn't be on me, the customer, to spend months of my life sifting through forums and struggling against the current, trying to get the game I paid money for to actually PLAY, I simply deleted both games from my computer and consoled myself only with the fact that I bought this one on sale. 
Still, it doesn't wash away the bad taste of the promise of a little video gamey fun being ruined by the video game not actually running.

Long - This game feels like it was made by fresh college grads-- which if it were, would actually be Super Impressive. Instead it's dull, unimaginative and definitely Not Funny. It was made around the time when the 80's outrun style was popular, but instead of doing anything interesting with the subject matter, just kind of kicks the can a bit. There's an attempt at using the super-masculine action hero trope in a parodic manner, but it just falls flat on its face. There's a joke about awful tutorials... that uses an awful tutorial to get it across. It's aggravating to play from the MAIN MENU -- seriously, for some reason the entire menu has to scroll in before it lets you use any of it. These all may sound like minor complaints, but all add up to a terrible user experience.

It's really difficult to choose weapons; the weapon wheel button is ALSO a shortcut to another weapon, so when the wheel opens you also equip another gun. It's hard to realise when you're on fire (which happens often), and the button to put out the flames is the same as to heal... which uses a healthpack-- so you may find yourself wasting heals because you mashed the button to put out the fire. 

Also pretty sure there was a lowkey transphobic sidequest not far into the game. Just... no. 

TL;DR -- If you REALLY REALLY like 80's action hero style jokes, Far Cry 3, and don't mind really crappy UX design, then buy this game. Everyone else steer clear.

[h1]A Deep Dive into Far Cry 3: Blood Dragon - A Furry Gamer's Perspective[/h1]

[h2]Introduction[/h2]
As an ice magic-wielding alpha wolf from HowlStrom, I'm no stranger to the depths of virtual worlds. My journey through countless digital realms has brought me to Ubisoft's peculiar creation, Far Cry 3: Blood Dragon. This game is a strange beast, seemingly pieced together from the neon-lit fragments of an era gone by. As a dedicated FPS gamer and a seasoned internet dweller, I found myself perplexed by its very existence. Buckle up, fellow furries and gamers, as I tear into this bewildering cyber-shooter.

[h2]Basic Plot Summary[/h2]
In a dystopian version of 2007, Sergeant Rex "Power" Colt, a Mark IV Cyber Commando, is dispatched to an unnamed island to stop a rogue colonel. The game's world is a retro-futuristic parody of 1980s action films, complete with cyborgs, mutant wildlife, and, of course, laser-shooting dinosaurs. It's a mix of every VHS-era cliché, thrown into a blender and served with a side of snarky one-liners.

[h2]Originality[/h2]
Original? Not in the slightest. Blood Dragon is an unapologetic homage to 80s pop culture, right down to its garish neon palette and synthwave soundtrack. It's as if someone vomited nostalgia all over Far Cry 3’s engine. But does that make it innovative? Hardly. It’s derivative to the core, wearing its influences on its sleeve without bringing anything genuinely new to the table.

[h2]The Studio[/h2]
Ubisoft Montreal, the studio behind this madness, has a reputation for pushing the boundaries. But with Blood Dragon, they seemed to have taken a bizarre detour. Known for their expansive and detailed open worlds, Ubisoft here decided to strip down and simplify. This game feels like a side project, a whimsical afterthought rather than a serious expansion.

[h2]Analysis/Evaluation[/h2]
Blood Dragon simplifies many of Far Cry 3’s mechanics. The crafting system is gone, replaced by a straightforward progression system. Combat feels clunky, and the over-the-top weapons lack the satisfying punch you'd expect. The titular Blood Dragons are more spectacle than substance, often serving as easy tools to clear enemy outposts rather than presenting a real challenge.

[h3]Character Development[/h3]
[b]Main Characters:[/b] Rex "Power" Colt is your stereotypical action hero, voiced by Michael Biehn. He’s a caricature, a hollow shell filled with recycled catchphrases. 
[b]Supporting Characters:[/b] Spider, Rex’s sidekick, is even less memorable. The villains are cartoonishly evil, lacking depth or motivation beyond world domination.
[b]Character Arcs and Relatability:[/b] There's no meaningful character development. Rex starts as a badass and ends as one. Any semblance of a narrative arc is drowned out by the game’s relentless attempt at humor.

[h3]Structure[/h3]
The game’s structure is typical of open-world shooters: liberate outposts, complete side missions, and collect upgrades. However, the main storyline is disappointingly linear and short. The side content does little to enrich the world or characters, making the game feel repetitive.

[h3]Impact[/h3]
Blood Dragon’s impact is purely aesthetic. Its retro style and humor might appeal to some, but it does little to advance the genre. It’s a shallow experience that relies heavily on its visual and auditory gimmicks.

[h3]Hook and Thesis[/h3]
The hook here is the 80s nostalgia. The thesis? Games can be fun and ridiculous. But does it deliver? Not really. The novelty wears off quickly, leaving behind a game that’s mechanically inferior to its predecessor.

[h2]Praise and Critique[/h2]
[b]Praise:[/b] The soundtrack by Power Glove is undeniably cool, perfectly capturing the retro vibe. The visuals, while garish, are distinctive.
[b]Critique:[/b] The humor is hit-or-miss, often relying on tired clichés. The gameplay, stripped of Far Cry 3’s complexities, feels shallow and unengaging. Blood Dragons, the game’s marquee feature, are underwhelming in practice.

[h2]Personal Opinion[/h2]
[b]Enjoyment:[/b] As an ice wolf who’s seen it all, I found myself quickly bored. The game’s charm fades fast, leaving behind a hollow shell of neon and noise.
[b]Highlights and Drawbacks:[/b] The initial thrill of the retro aesthetic was a highlight, but the lack of depth and repetitive gameplay were major drawbacks.

[h3]Evaluation[/h3]
Blood Dragon is a novelty, a quirky experiment that lacks the substance of a full-fledged game. It’s a distraction, not a destination.

[h3]Comparison[/h3]
[b]Similar Games:[/b] Compare it to games like Duke Nukem Forever or Serious Sam, and you’ll find Blood Dragon lacking in both humor and gameplay depth. Even compared to its parent game, Far Cry 3, it feels like a shallow spin-off.

[h2]Overall Conclusion[/h2]
Far Cry 3: Blood Dragon is a perplexing creation. It’s a game that leans heavily on nostalgia and parody but fails to deliver a satisfying gaming experience. For hardcore FPS fans and game nerds, it’s a disappointing detour. As Kiba Snowpaw, I’ve seen better games lost in the icy winds of HowlStrom. Save your time and play something with more substance. Blood Dragon might have a neon glow, but it’s as cold and hollow as the winter nights on my home planet.

As often, I wish there were more rating options than just thumbs down or up. I enjoyed playing this game, but there was also the impression that the creators and producers restricted themselves to modest aspirations. In other words, the game lacks content. There are basically only four characters with a name - the protagonist, a tragic loss, one ally and the foe. The nature of their relationships are set after the introductory level and don't change - there is not even a "Ha I only used you to get rid of my opponent and now I betray you"-moment. Furthermore, there a few weapons, no minigames and small variety in the side missions. Plot and story are so flat that they rather imitate 80s Sci-Fi-Action-flicks than poking fun at them. Though there are some funny moments, they are restricted to some dialogue lines. For the final, a cheesy approach was chosen, but I would have preferred an ironical twist - like for example, that a nobody would become a hero and Rex Power Colt would be de-glorified.

Combatwise, there is not so much a lack of content but simply of enemies - it is possible (and quickly happens accidentally) to shoot an enemy from a corner and then watch how the whole garnison of 15-20 foes approaches you in "waves" of 1-2 people, allowing you to take them out easily one after another. Though I played on hard, my Rex died less than five times during the whole game and I would not call myself a pro. So either there should be more enemies or they should have a better AI and target more precisely.

This problem even worsens once you have some of the upgrades. While the enemies are the same from the beginning to the end, Rex can (by finishing the side missions) acquire overpowered weapons. Especially the sniper rifle at full modification allows you to take out most enemies with a body shot (and often killing nearby ones, too, because the bullets become explosive) at a very wide range and even with the swaying of the scope practically eliminated.

Of course, you could also argue that it's only consequent that you are overpowered since the framework is a pseudo-manly and dim lit action title from the 80s. This leads me back to the observation that Far Cry 3: Blood Dragon is more a copy than a parody of the underlying matter.

What I liked was the movement, the sound track and the visual style overall. They were worth investing 14 hours at a time where I had absolutely nothing better to do. I really think that this game could have been much better if the humour was more drastic, consequent and widespread and if there was at least some character development and an actual plot. That way, I would have wanted more than just 14 hours.

Far Cry: Blood Dragon DLC – A Disappointing and Detached Experience

As a huge fan of Far Cry 3, I was genuinely excited to dive into Far Cry: Blood Dragon, but unfortunately, this DLC felt more like a completely different game than an expansion of the core experience. It has nothing to do with the gripping story and immersive world of the main campaign. Instead, it presents a bizarre, 80s-inspired neon nightmare that feels like a cash grab rather than a meaningful addition to the Far Cry universe.

First off, the story—or rather, the lack of it—is just a mess. There’s no emotional connection to the characters, no real plotline to follow. The dialogue tries too hard to be campy and nostalgic, but it comes off as shallow and obnoxious. It’s not even remotely engaging compared to the fantastic narrative we got in Far Cry 3. What could’ve been an interesting continuation of the world just feels like a bizarre, unoriginal spin-off.

The enemies are boring and uncreative. Gone are the varied, dynamic foes that kept you on your toes in the main game. Here, it’s all about the same old enemies with a neon glow, and they’re not even fun to fight. Without any real tactics or variety, combat quickly becomes repetitive and tedious.

To make matters worse, the map feels empty and lifeless. In Far Cry 3, the island was filled with things to explore, dangers to face, and secrets to uncover. In Blood Dragon, it’s just vast, desolate terrain with very little to do. Sure, there are collectables scattered around, but they feel pointless—there’s no real incentive to go out of your way for them unless you’re a completionist.

If you’re not someone who feels the need to hunt down every last item on the map, then don’t even bother. The DLC doesn’t offer much beyond that. Without a meaningful story or interesting side activities, there’s just nothing here to keep you engaged. It feels like the developers slapped together a quick cash-in instead of delivering a DLC that adds value to the Far Cry experience.

In short, Far Cry: Blood Dragon is a forgettable, disconnected experience that fails to live up to the legacy of Far Cry 3. If you’re expecting anything even remotely related to the main campaign’s story, you’ll be severely disappointed. Save your time and money.

It's an ok game, but after playing this i know i don't want to play any of the other Far Cries (and i haven't). It is bland and repetitive. Story missions and the theme is ok, but nothing really engaging, spectacular, at times stupid even. I get that this was an intention to beat on trash movies cliches, but it was too much some times. Outside of the main story it is an open world which is pretty empty. Yeah with some fights between scientists and commandos going on here and there. It was fun to roam in a jeep, but not for long. Side quest are all similar (go and kill someone and maybe save some scientist jerk). I hated missions requiring you to do stealth in an open field surrounded by 20+ enemies. "Cutscenes" were often too long and, i don't know, i just didn't liked how they sounded and looked. I didn't get the leveling thing as you couldn't choose a skill, it was just a linear progression which happened automatically. I hated some animations like pilfering cyberhearts (which you needed sometimes to distract dragons) or shotgun reloading cycle which took to long to start shooting again.

Then the general design. Saves somethimes weren't working. So i ended up only using checkpoints. And once i had to listen to some story dialog like 10 times while dying on some side quest and loading again. Stupid system of repeating everything when you load a save. After a recent uPlay update it started to mess with Blood Dragon launch and jumped in front of it making BD starting in a windowed state, so i had to restart it every time (that' because uPlay wasn't already running, yeah, i don't want some program to run all the time when i only need it for one game occasionally). That's another point why i won't play Far Cry or other Ubisoft game.

All in all, it was fun to shoot enemies and ride the jeep at times, but it was also a bland, sometimes boring game with an overdone humour. Can't call it a good game.

I feel more angry about it now after collecting my thoughts than when I was playing the game.

First off, the gameplay is almost exactly the same as Far Cry 3 because it's running in the same engine. The open world is completely new though, and so is the leveling system and the way weapon upgrades are earned. Having a smaller open world and a more straightforward leveling and weapon upgrade system is actually something I think this game does better than the main game. The smaller map meant I was getting into combat more often and the simplified leveling system meant that I didn't spend nearly as much time in menus, and I actually had some incentive to clear out strongholds and complete sidequests due to them being the way to unlock weapon upgrades. Also, the addition of dinosaurs that shoot lasers out of their eyes and take a ton of bullets to put down made me feel truly unsafe when traveling.

The overabundance of cash and the repetitiveness of all of the sidequests is still an issue here though. There is absolutely no variety here. Each side mission is "kill the enemy before a hostage dies", and the enemies almost never go after the hostage and instead just attack you so there's basically no real difference between them and the stronghold liberation objectives. And the island itself has no memorable landmarks or discerning features. Everything just sort of blurs together into this ugly looking, dark, neon red and blue mess. The soundtrack's alright though.

The story is bad, but in an intentional, tounge-in-cheek way. It's clearly taking cues from 80s action movies of all quality, including Predator and Miami Connection (which to the game's credit, actually got a chuckle out of me when that song played at the end). The problem is the dialogue feels like the Asylum movie studio tried to make a video game. I [i] hate [/i] Asylum or other intentionally bad movies. It's not funny to purposefully be bad, it's just grating. And good lord, was Michael Biehn's performance grating. I know the guy can be great, I saw The Terminator and Aliens. But he just feels so checked out for his role as Rex, and the overly explicit one-liners like "dickshitter" made me cringe into a singularity even back when I had tried playing this game on release.

The writing in general has this early 2010s "so randum" internet humor stink about it. There is an actual "Imma firin' mah lazor" reference, which is the worst of it, but this is the level we're on. This, on top of openly making fun of bad story or gameplay elements while still doing them (like the forced tutorial), just made me want to uninstall. The only reason I didn't is because the game is mercifully short. There's only a handful of main story missions and the whole thing can be completed in about 3-8 hours depending on how much side content you do. If this kind of humor doesn't bother you then maybe you'll enjoy this game, but otherwise you'll probably hate it.

If you enjoyed [i]Far Cry 3[/i]: Go for it. However, as I did not, I cannot justify giving this a positive rating. I do think this is a better game as it cuts out some of the tedium that presented itself in [i]FC3[/i] (although it is not completely free from it as you have to grind side-missions to get weapon upgrades and whatnot) mainly thanks to the smaller map. The whole "80’s" aesthetic has been so played out by now (although slightly less so back when this was released, I suppose) but the presentation is overall appealing enough with its charming cutscenes and original score. It is with the gameplay where I once again have issues. Despite Ubisoft’s best attempts at creating a faux-old school aesthetic the game is the same cookie-cutter structure as most of their singleplayer games post-[i]Assassin’s Creed 2[/i]. A big, yet empty, map with a bunch of markers that, at the end of the day, creates tedium rather than engaging content. The shooting is the typical hitscan garbage we have gotten used to (which is rather problematic when the enviorments are this large and empty...) and the stealth is just as undercooked as usual (meaning that there is just a quarter circle that fills up and a giant neon sign is magically attached to the player once you get detected). There is nothing old school about the actual gameplay no matter how cute the introductory parody on modern tutorials may be. At least you are not tortured by the presence of Jason Brody this time around.
